name: Orange juice / vitamin C diet

lead: This practice means taking in large amounts of orange juice or vitamin C to firm and brighten the skin.

The chain: vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that build collagen, and collagen is what gives skin its firmness. That established role is the basis for the appearance claims. No published trial has tested mega-dose orange juice for skin, so whether intake beyond adequacy changes how skin looks has not been studied. Wikipedia describes the health value of orange juice as debatable because of its high sugar content.

paras: People drink orange juice daily or take vitamin C, often alongside other citrus and fruit. Skin changes are reported over weeks.
Doses above about 3,000 mg/day have caused diarrhea and other gastrointestinal effects, and the US upper level is 2,000 mg/day. Orange juice is high in sugar.

angle.text: Users drink orange juice or take large amounts of vitamin C to support collagen and brighten skin. Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis, which is the route to firmer-looking skin. Whether high intake changes appearance has not been tested.

lead: The orange juice or vitamin C diet is a practice of drinking large amounts of citrus juice, or taking high amounts of vitamin C, with the aim of a brighter, healthier-looking complexion. The reasoning is that vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that build stable collagen, the protein that gives skin firmness, so people who want firmer, glowing skin try to keep their intake high.[1]

Orange juice is a convenient source: a 250 mL cup provides a large share of daily vitamin C along with about 21 g of sugar.[2] Some community members treat juice as an add-on to protein-heavy or low-carbohydrate eating, while others discuss it as mostly sugar with some vitamin C.[3]

Reference sources describe the US recommended intake as 90 mg/day for men and 75 mg/day for women, and note that absorption efficiency falls at large doses and excess is excreted in urine.[1] No published trial has tested orange-juice-centred protocols for skin appearance.

paras: A 250 mL cup of orange juice has about 112 calories and 21 g of sugar and is a rich source of vitamin C.[2] Oranges and lemons contain roughly 53 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, and pasteurisation and cooking reduce the content of foods.[1]

Vitamin C is needed for enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, and prolonged deficiency causes scurvy.[1] Active transport absorbs most vitamin C at ordinary intakes, absorption efficiency falls at large doses, and plasma levels saturate at modest intakes.[1]
Orange juice also contains flavonoids, and reviews have discussed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of orange juice in general.[4]

On looksmax.org, orange juice appears in diet threads where members weigh its vitamin C against its sugar and carbohydrate content, and in light-hearted questions about whether drinking it counts as improving looks.[3]

No studies found on orange-juice-centred diets for skin appearance. Trials of orange juice in other settings include a randomized trial of flavonoid-rich orange juice in young adults with depression and a trial of daily orange consumption in fatty liver disease, which did not look at skin.[5][6]

The US Institute of Medicine set a 2,000 mg/day upper level in 2000 based on gastrointestinal effects seen above 3,000 mg/day, while the European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence to set one.[1] Orange juice is acidic and sugar-rich, and some government guidance favours whole fruit over juice.[2]

lore.intro: Online, citrus and vitamin C are discussed for brighter skin, with members debating juice against whole foods and supplements.[3]
